title: The butter thief
hook: a toddler with butter on his chin, a line of happy monkeys, and the neighbors at his mother's door

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raksha Bandhan: a thread on a wrist, and a promise back. Your line was a thread can hold a promise. Today, the man who held Arjuna's reins, back when he was small enough to steal butter. Day eighty-five.

A village of cowherds on the banks of the Yamuna, early morning. The women have been churning since before dawn, and the fresh butter is hung high in clay pots, out of reach. It doesn't help. By noon a pot is cracked, the butter is gone, and a line of monkeys is licking their fingers. The culprit is about three years old. He has butter on his chin, and he swears he was asleep. The women march to his mother's door to complain, and halfway through complaining, they start laughing. Today: the butter thief.
screen: `BUTTER, HUNG OUT OF REACH.` → `A LINE OF HAPPY MONKEYS.` → `HE SWEARS HE WAS ASLEEP.`

segments.voice: The boy is Krishna, the same Krishna you left holding Arjuna's reins on day seventy-seven. The Bhagavata Purana gives the neighbors' complaint almost as a list. He lets the calves loose before milking time. He steals the curd and the butter. He feeds it to the monkeys, and if the monkeys won't eat, he breaks the pot. When the pots are hung out of reach, he stacks up stools and a mortar and climbs. And when he's caught, he looks so innocent that nobody can stay angry. That's why the nickname stuck. In Hindi he's Makhan Chor, the butter thief, and it's always said with love. Here's what surprises many people. This same Krishna is honored as God. In the Gita he speaks as the source of everything, and in the same life he's a toddler being scolded by his mother. Devotees don't treat that as a contradiction. Many say it's the point: God close enough to be fed, chased, scolded and loved like a child. So Krishna comes with many faces. The baby born in a prison at midnight. The butter thief. The cowherd boy whose flute pulls the whole village outside. The friend driving a chariot onto a battlefield. Many people love one face most. In many homes there's a small brass baby Krishna, crawling, a sweet in one hand, often called Laddu Gopal. Families bathe him, dress him and offer him food each day, the way you'd care for a little child. Gopala means a cowherd, the one who looks after the cows. And the butter? Some devotees say it stands for a soft, well-churned heart, and that a heart is what he really comes to steal.
screen: `A THIEF THE WHOLE VILLAGE LOVES.` · `THE SAME KRISHNA, HONORED AS GOD.` · `ONE PERSON, MANY FACES.` · `THE BABY ON THE HOME SHRINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture someone small you love, caught mid-mischief. A child, a little brother or sister, a pet. Sit, and breathe. See the face the moment they're caught: the wide eyes, the guilty grin, the evidence on their chin. Notice what happens in you. Annoyance, maybe, and right under it, something softer. Stay with the softer thing. If you pray, you can hold Krishna's child face in your mind the same way. The bell holds the time.
Makhan Chor. The butter thief: Krishna as a little boy, scolded and adored, and still honored as God. Today's word.
Your line: close enough to scold. A God you can chase around the kitchen. Day eighty-five.

howItsDone: Many Hindu homes keep a small image of baby Krishna, often called Laddu Gopal, and bathe, dress and offer food to him each day; the butter-thief stories are told and sung, especially around Janmashtami.

fork.setup: you're Yashoda. the neighbors are at your door listing what your toddler stole. he's standing behind you with butter on his chin, swearing he was asleep. what happens?
options: you punish him in front of everyone.
you try to scold him, and everyone ends up laughing.
you pay the neighbors back and say nothing.
fork.reveal: in the Bhagavata, the complaints pile up, but his innocent face wins. nobody can stay angry with him for long.

original.note: Hindi: makhan, butter, and chor, thief. Krishna's best-loved childhood nickname.
